meta.triageRationale: One story in one module with one clear approach: the approved spec already fixes which theme variable each component uses, so what is left is replacing colour values in three style sources and adding a check that no fixed colour remains.

findings.premise: Every element of the approved mapping in SPEC-3d2161bcef24cecf has a name in the layer, including the markdown group 'textPreformat.*, textCodeBlock.background, textBlockQuote.* and textSeparator.foreground'.
findings.evidence: The spec maps markdown to 'textPreformat.*' (foreground and background). The layer defines only `--pre-fg: var(--vscode-textPreformat-foreground)`; there is no name for textPreformat.background. The cause is the token set: markdown-style.ts:88-89 uses the single `codeBg` field for both inline code (`.insrc-md code{...background:${t.codeBg}`) and fenced blocks (`.insrc-md pre{background:${t.codeBg}`), and the design points `codeBg` at the code-block ground, so inline code chips get textCodeBlock.background instead of textPreformat.background. Every other mapping entry I compared (bars, bubbles, tool row, markers, diff, approval, buttons, decided chips, selection card, input, selects, pill, attachment chips, progress, quote, separator, focus) has a name. [files: docs/standalone/dev-chat-follows-vs-code-theme-E202610133d2161bc/SPEC.md, vscode-plugin/src/chat/markdown-style.ts]
findings.action: Add a `--pre-bg: var(--vscode-textPreformat-background)` name and an override rule for inline code (`.insrc-md code{background:var(--pre-bg)}` with `.insrc-md pre code` kept at none) among the rules the shell adds after the markdown rules, or record explicitly that inline code takes the code-block ground and why.

findings.premise: No non-goal is built: layout, shapes and glyphs are unchanged, the docs-review panel is untouched, and the font change is limited to the theme's monospace editor font.
findings.evidence: The design changes colour values only, plus one wrapper span for the history chip whose border, radius and icon position are kept. The docs-review panel is fed only by renderTerminalStyle and DOCS_REVIEW_MARKDOWN_TOKENS (docs-review-panel.ts:1222, 1489), neither of which is changed. One caveat: the design's default for `--sans` is `var(--vscode-font-family)` (the interface font), while the spec says 'Fonts are the theme's monospace editor font' and lists 'Changing fonts other than taking the theme's monospace editor font' as a non-goal. The design does not hide this: it raises it as the open question, and today's prose font is indeed a fixed sans stack (chat-panel.ts:597, markdown-style.ts:77, 100).
findings.action: Resolve the open question before planning. If the answer is not the editor font, the spec's font wording needs the user's explicit change, since the default as written contradicts it.

findings.premise: Today the shell forces a dark colour scheme and chooses colours from 19 named variables holding fixed values, with further fixed tints, gradients and fixed code grounds in its rules, the row renderer's style and the markdown tokens.
findings.evidence: chat-panel.ts:594-597 is `:root{color-scheme:dark;--font:...;--bg:#0b0e14;...--sans:'Inter',...}` with exactly 19 names (font, bg, bg-alt, bg-inset, panel, fg, fg-strong, muted, dim, border, border-lit, accent, accent2, amber, magenta, red, user, sel, sans). Fixed values outside :root: radial gradients on body (599) and #insrc-term (610), the dot's box-shadow (605), the pill border (669), diff lines (691-692), user bubble (707), `#0a0d14` on .insrc-toolrow (712) and .insrc-json (722). render-registry.ts:201-250 holds rgba tints, linear-gradient tints, hex text colours, `#0a0d14` and literal fallbacks (`var(--border,#222a36)`, `var(--muted,#9aa3ad)`, `var(--font,monospace)`). markdown-style.ts:110 is `codeBg: '#0a0d14'`.

findings.premise: Today the history chip is the select itself, with a faint fixed fill and a clock icon painted as an SVG data URI whose stroke is a fixed colour.
findings.evidence: chat-panel.ts:685-688: `.chrome #insrc-history{...background-color:rgba(255,255,255,.045);border:1px solid var(--border);border-radius:6px;background-image:url("data:image/svg+xml,...stroke='%23c6cdd8'..."),linear-gradient(...),linear-gradient(...)`. The markup at 943 is a bare `<select id="insrc-history" class="segsel ...">` inside `<span class="right">`.

findings.premise: The shared token sheet supplies the marker glyphs and the chat only re-tones them; the sheet maps nine roles to theme variables with literal fallbacks.
findings.evidence: design-tokens.ts:220-224 sets `content: var(--it-mk-*)` on the marker ::before rules; chat-panel.ts:616-620 overrides only the colour with `!important`. design-tokens.ts:184-194 emits nine `var(--vscode-*, literal)` roles (font, bg, fg, dim, accent, warn, err, sel, border). Worth knowing when building: the shell emits `${style}${layoutStyle}` (928) and the body is `<body class="insrc-term">` (935), so the shared rule `.insrc-term{font-family;font-size;line-height;background;color}` outranks the shell's `body{...}` rule by specificity. The body's own font, size and ground therefore already come from the shared sheet, not from `--font`/`--bg`.
findings.action: None required. The builder should not expect the `body{}` declarations to be what the panel shows; the `.box` and descendant rules are what take effect.

findings.premise: The decided badge can get its own passed and failed colours through `.insrc-permoutcome__badge.insrc-approval__btn--approve` and `--deny` without changing the renderer's class names.
findings.evidence: render-registry.ts:525 builds the badge as `badge.className='insrc-permoutcome__badge insrc-approval__btn--'+(approved?'approve':'deny')`, so both classes are on the same element and the two-class selector matches and outranks the single-class button rules at 222-223.

findings.premise: The markdown token set has no field for a block quote ground, a separate rule colour or a separate link colour, so those must be added by the shell after the markdown rules while renderMarkdownStyle stays unchanged.
findings.evidence: markdown-style.ts:86 gives the block quote only a left border and text colour; 92 draws `hr` from `t.border`; 88 and 91 both use `t.accent` for inline code text and for links. Pointing `accent` at the preformat foreground therefore also recolours links, which the design corrects with a later `.insrc-md a` rule. chat-panel.ts:720 emits the markdown rules inside layoutStyle, so rules appended after it win at equal specificity.

findings.premise: A masked icon given as a data URI is allowed by the existing content security policy, and the existing policy test will still see it.
findings.evidence: chat-panel.ts:585: `default-src 'none'; img-src data:; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; script-src 'nonce-...'`. Mask images are fetched under img-src, which permits data:. The existing test (chat-panel.test.ts:1508-1516) collects every `url(` scheme across all style blocks, not only background-image, so a `mask-image:url("data:...")` keeps both its non-vacuous guard and its policy check.

findings.premise: The three listed files are the only places the chat's colours are set: RENDER_REGISTRY_STYLE and CHAT_MARKDOWN_TOKENS have no other consumer, and no colour is set from script.
findings.evidence: RENDER_REGISTRY_STYLE is consumed only at chat-panel.ts:698 (tests aside); CHAT_MARKDOWN_TOKENS only at chat-panel.ts:720. A search of chat-panel.ts, render-registry.ts and transcript-pager.ts for `.style`, cssText and style attributes finds only `bar.style.display` in transcript-pager.ts:66-67. The chat's names appear nowhere else in non-test source (docs-review-panel.ts:1496 only mentions them in a comment). The mock generator (mocks/gen-mocks.ts) does not render the chat shell.

findings.premise: The existing tests that need changing are 'the four assertions that pinned the history chip's old fill and icon stroke'.
findings.evidence: Only two assertions pin the fill and stroke (1463 `background-color:rgba\(255,255,255,\.045\)`, 1477 `stroke='%23c6cdd8'`). Moving the border, radius, ground and icon from the select to a wrapper with a ::before mask breaks more, in two tests. Test at 1119 ('...the rest of the chip is untouched') asserts on the `.chrome #insrc-history{...}` rule: 1127 `border:1px solid var\(--border\)`, 1128 `border-radius:6px`, 1129 `padding:3px 16px 3px 22px`, 1130 `background-position:left 6px center`. Test at 1449 asserts on the same rule: 1455 `background-image:url\("data:image\/svg\+xml,`, 1456 `background-repeat:no-repeat,no-repeat,no-repeat` (three layers), 1461 border, 1462 radius, 1466-1475 the padding and `background-position:left (\d+)px center` relationship. Roughly ten assertions across two tests pin where the chip's border, radius and icon live, not four. [files: vscode-plugin/src/chat/__tests__/chat-panel.test.ts]
findings.action: Replace the migration step's count with the real inventory: both tests (chat-panel.test.ts:1119-1131 and 1449-1483) must be rewritten to assert the border, radius and ground on the wrapper, the icon as a mask in its ::before placed inside the left padding, and the select's own rule reduced to max-width, padding and the two arrow layers. Keep the intent of each (one control, icon inside the padding, 36ch cap).

findings.premise: Nothing stored changes and the docs-review panel's document stays byte-identical, because it does not share any of the three changed sources.
findings.evidence: docs-review-panel.ts:14 and 19 import only renderTerminalStyle, DOCS_REVIEW_MARKDOWN_TOKENS and renderMarkdownStyle; 1489 builds its markdown rules from DOCS_REVIEW_MARKDOWN_TOKENS and its own rules use `--it-*` only. It does not import RENDER_REGISTRY_STYLE or CHAT_MARKDOWN_TOKENS. The design leaves renderMarkdownStyle, DOCS_REVIEW_MARKDOWN_TOKENS and design-tokens.ts unchanged, and the change touches only CSS strings, so no transcript row, message or setting shape is involved.

findings.premise: Every optional theme variable falls back to a variable every theme defines, so no element loses its ground or border when a theme leaves one unset.
findings.evidence: VS Code's colour registry is not in this repository, so I could not check which variables are always emitted. The fallback chains as written are well formed. One case to confirm: as far as I recall, high-contrast themes leave both diffEditor.insertedLineBackground and diffEditor.insertedTextBackground unset (they use borders instead), and likewise for the removed pair. If so `--add-bg` and `--del-bg` have no value there and the diff's added and removed lines are drawn with no ground at all (chat-panel.ts:691-692 give them nothing else to tell them apart). The result is a transparent line, not a broken one, but the design's statement that the fallback is 'a variable every theme defines' would be untrue for these two names.
findings.action: Check the diff line grounds in a high-contrast theme during the smoke test. If they are unset, state the expected high-contrast look for diff lines in the edge cases (for example a contrast-border edge), and narrow the test's claim about fallbacks accordingly.

findings.premise: The colour scheme can follow the theme-kind class on the body: light for vscode-light and vscode-high-contrast-light, dark for vscode-dark and vscode-high-contrast.
findings.evidence: The classes are added by VS Code at run time, not by this repository: the shell emits only `<body class="insrc-term">` (chat-panel.ts:935, pinned by chat-panel.test.ts:1243), and no file under vscode-plugin/src mentions the vscode-light or vscode-dark classes. From memory, a high-contrast light webview body carries both `vscode-high-contrast-light` and `vscode-high-contrast` (kept for compatibility). If that is right, a `body.vscode-high-contrast{color-scheme:dark}` rule also matches high-contrast light, and the result depends on rule order.
findings.action: Write the light high-contrast rule after the dark high-contrast rule (or exclude it with `:not(.vscode-high-contrast-light)`), say so in the design, and have the unit test assert that order. Confirm in the smoke check with a high-contrast light theme, which the smoke subject should name explicitly.

findings.premise: Each acceptance criterion (ac1, ac2, ac3) maps to at least one named test, and the tests can be written the way the strategy says: the shell rendered through createChatPanelHost with a fake channel, with the chat's own style separable from the shared token sheet.
findings.evidence: The LLD's acceptanceMapping (LLD-7fefc3fc5c51793e-S001.json:237-256) gives ac1 two unit tests and the smoke check, ac2 one unit test and ac3 two integration tests. chat-panel.test.ts:117 and chat-shell.test.ts:45 already render the shell through `createChatPanelHost({ createPanel: () => channel, ... })`. The shell emits the shared sheet and the chat's own style as two separate `<style>` blocks (`${style}${layoutStyle}`, chat-panel.ts:928), so a test can scan the second alone. Two things for the builder: the attachment rules are emitted only when the host has the attachment seams (chat-panel.ts:653-668), so the scan must render a host with attachments on or `.attchip` goes unchecked; and ac1's 'follows the theme' rests in part on the smoke check, which the gate cannot run.
findings.action: Render the shell with the attachment seams present in the colour-scan and name-defined tests, and record the smoke result as reported by the builder.

summary.prose: The dev chat's colours are chosen in one list of named values at the top of its style. Today that list holds fixed dark colours; this Story points each name at a VS Code theme variable, adds names for the surfaces the approved mapping needs, and replaces every remaining fixed colour, tint and gradient in the chat's three style sources with one of those names. The chat then follows light, dark and high-contrast themes. Layout, shapes and glyphs stay as they are, and the docs-review panel is not touched.

hldContextSlice.frameworkSummary: Standalone feature — no parent HLD. Design directly against the repo, grounded on the s1 analyze passes. There are no HLD shared contracts to honour.

boundary.internal: Make the dev chat follow the VS Code theme

api.name: RENDER_REGISTRY_STYLE
api.signature: export const RENDER_REGISTRY_STYLE: string  // existing constant in render-registry.ts; same selectors, colour values changed

returns.meaning: The row renderer's rules. Every colour is `var(--<name>)` from the shell's named layer; there is no hex, rgb/rgba, hsl, color-mix or gradient, and no `var(--name, literal)` fallback. Approval card: warning ground and border. Approve button: button ground and text; deny button: secondary button ground and text; hover uses the theme's hover grounds in place of a brightness filter. Approved and rejected card states: border in the passed or failed colour on the code-block ground. Permission-outcome chip, resolved selection card and selection-outcome chip: code-block ground with the widget border. Decided badge: passed or failed colour for text and border on a transparent ground, given by the more specific selectors `.insrc-permoutcome__badge.insrc-approval__btn--approve` and `--deny`, so the renderer's class names do not change. Selection card: widget ground and border; option rows: checkbox ground and border; chosen option: focus border; control glyph: checkbox foreground; confirm: button ground and text.

preconditions: The document that embeds it defines the named layer (the chat shell does).
postconditions: Selectors, box model, spacing, radii and class names are unchanged.

api.name: CHAT_MARKDOWN_TOKENS
api.signature: export const CHAT_MARKDOWN_TOKENS: MarkdownStyleTokens  // existing token set in markdown-style.ts; values changed, type unchanged

returns.meaning: Each field holds a name from the shell's layer: text and headings the editor foreground, borders the panel border, muted the description foreground, `accent` (inline code text) the preformat foreground, `codeBg` the code-block ground in place of the fixed '#0a0d14', `fontMono` the editor font. `fontSans` (the assistant's prose) stays `var(--sans)`; what `--sans` holds is the open question. renderMarkdownStyle and DOCS_REVIEW_MARKDOWN_TOKENS are not changed; rules the token set has no field for (block quote ground and border, horizontal rule, link colour) are added by the chat shell after the markdown rules.

postconditions: The docs-review panel's markdown is byte-identical to today.

dataModelChanges.entity: the chat shell's named colour layer (the `:root` rule of layoutStyle in renderShell, chat-panel.ts)
dataModelChanges.details: The one place the chat's colours are chosen. `color-scheme:dark` is removed; the colour scheme follows the theme-kind class VS Code puts on the body (light for vscode-light and vscode-high-contrast-light, dark for vscode-dark and vscode-high-contrast). Every existing name is kept and now holds a theme variable; names are added for the roles the mapping needs. A fallback is always another theme variable, never a literal. Every border name starts with the high-contrast border so high-contrast themes get their outline.

dataModelChanges.entity: the shell's own rules (layoutStyle in renderShell, chat-panel.ts)
dataModelChanges.details: Every fixed colour outside `:root` is replaced by a name. Removed: the two radial gradients on body and the one on #insrc-term (flat grounds), and the header dot's glow (the dot stays, in --accent). The auto-approve pill's border and text use --warn. The diff's added and removed lines use --add-bg and --del-bg; its buttons use the secondary button names. The user bubble uses --user-bg and --user-border; the assistant bubble uses --panel with --border-lit. .insrc-toolrow and .insrc-json use --code-bg with --border-lit. Links use --link. The input's text uses --input-fg and its placeholder --placeholder. The progress dots use --progress. The status bar selects' option lists use the dropdown names. Focusable controls get a --focus outline on :focus-visible. Rules for block quotes, horizontal rules and links inside the assistant's markdown are added after the markdown rules. The select arrows stay two linear gradients built from --muted and `transparent`: they draw a shape, not a tint.

dataModelChanges.entity: the history chip in the header (markup and rule in renderShell, chat-panel.ts)
dataModelChanges.details: Today the chip is the select itself: a faint fixed fill, and the clock icon painted as an SVG data URI whose stroke is a fixed colour, which a theme variable cannot reach. The select is wrapped in one span that carries the chip's border, radius and ground (the dropdown ground) and draws the icon in its ::before as a mask filled with the current text colour, so the icon follows the theme. The select keeps its id, options, arrow and behaviour; the icon's shape and position are unchanged. The mask is a data URI, which the existing `img-src data:` allows; the content security policy is not changed.

errorCases.scenario: A theme does not define a variable the chat uses (an optional colour the theme leaves unset, or a variable an older VS Code does not have, such as the chat request ground).
errorCases.detection: Nothing in code can see it at run time: the browser treats a declaration whose var() has no value as unset. It is prevented by construction: every name whose theme variable is optional carries a fallback to a variable every theme defines, and a test checks that each such name has one.
errorCases.response: The fallback variable is used: the user message falls back to the inactive selection ground, widget and request borders fall back to the panel border, diff line grounds fall back to the diff text grounds.
errorCases.userImpact: The element is drawn in a neighbouring theme colour instead of losing its ground or taking the text colour as its border.

errorCases.scenario: A rule refers to a name the layer does not define (a typo, or a name removed from the list).
errorCases.detection: A test collects every `var(--name)` used in the shell's style, the row renderer's style and the chat's markdown rules and fails when a name that is not a --vscode-* variable is missing from the layer.

errorCases.scenario: A fixed colour is reintroduced later (a hex, an rgb/rgba or hsl value, a color-mix, a tint gradient, or a `var(--x, literal)` fallback).
errorCases.detection: A test scans the chat's own style in the rendered shell (everything except the shared token sheet, which is out of scope) and fails on any of those forms; linear-gradient is allowed only when built from names and `transparent`.

errorCases.scenario: A theme variable name is misspelt, so the element silently loses its colour.
errorCases.detection: A test compares the set of --vscode-* variables the layer refers to with the list in the approved mapping; a variable outside that list fails.
errorCases.userImpact: None: it cannot ship. A name that is spelt as approved but does not exist in VS Code can only be seen in the panel, which the smoke check covers.

edgeCases.expected: Light grounds and dark text everywhere, including the status bar selects' option lists and the scrollbars, because the colour scheme follows the theme kind; no dark panel remains.
Every bordered element is outlined with the theme's contrast border; user and assistant messages are told apart by their outlines, labels and alignment even where their grounds are the same.

edgeCases.input: The user switches theme while the chat is open.
edgeCases.expected: The chat repaints at once with no reload, since every colour is a variable VS Code updates in place.

edgeCases.input: A theme whose terminal colours are close to its background.
edgeCases.expected: Markers are less distinct in that theme; this follows the user's decision to take marker colours from the theme's terminal palette.

edgeCases.input: A theme whose warning ground is opaque and strong.
edgeCases.expected: The approval card is drawn in it with the editor's text colour; the card's title uses the warning foreground. Whether that pair reads well is a property of the theme.

edgeCases.input: A restored chat with every kind of row (messages, tool rows and results, diff, approval outcomes, selection outcomes, attachments, markdown with code, quote, table and rule).
edgeCases.expected: Every row is drawn from theme colours; nothing shows a leftover dark ground.
Unchanged: its document is byte-identical to today.

edgeCases.input: The chat host built with a custom renderStyle or theme (as tests and mocks do).
edgeCases.expected: Unchanged behaviour: the shell's own layer does not depend on the injected sheet.

invariantsToPreserve.text: The shell stays one nonce'd inline script and one content security policy, `default-src 'none'; img-src data:; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; script-src 'nonce-...'`; every image source the shell declares is a data URI.
Selectors, class names, element ids, the box model, spacing, radii, glyphs and the markup the tests address stay as they are, apart from the one wrapper around the history select.
The row renderer's class names and structure are unchanged; only RENDER_REGISTRY_STYLE's colour values change.
renderMarkdownStyle, DOCS_REVIEW_MARKDOWN_TOKENS and design-tokens.ts are not changed, so the docs-review panel and the generated mocks are byte-identical.
The shared token sheet keeps supplying the marker glyphs to the chat; the chat only re-tones them.

chat theme: the named layer refers only to the theme variables of the approved mapping, and every optional one falls back to another theme variable

chat theme: each component uses the name the mapping gives it (bars, transcript, user and assistant bubbles, tool row, markers, diff lines, approval card and buttons, decided badge, selection card, input, selects, pill, attachment chips, progress, markdown)
chat theme: selectors, class names and element ids of the shell and the row renderer are the same as before the change, and the shell is still one nonce'd inline script under the same policy
chat theme: the docs-review panel's rendered document, the shared token sheet and the docs-review markdown rules are byte-identical to before the change

migration.stateBefore: The chat shell forces a dark colour scheme and chooses its colours from 19 named variables holding fixed values, with further fixed tints, gradients and three fixed code grounds in its rules, in the row renderer's style and in the chat's markdown tokens (s1: the chat shell's palette; s1: the row renderer's style and the chat's markdown tokens). The docs-review panel uses a separate shared sheet and its own markdown tokens (s1: what is shared with the docs-review panel).
migration.stateAfter: The same names hold VS Code theme variables, new names cover the roles of the approved mapping, no fixed colour, tint or decorative gradient remains in the chat's three style sources, and the colour scheme follows the theme kind. The history chip's icon is a mask in the text colour inside one wrapper. The docs-review panel and the shared sheet are unchanged.

migrationSteps.action: Point the existing names in the shell's layer at theme variables, add the new names, remove the forced dark colour scheme and add the theme-kind colour scheme rules. Rules that already use names follow at once.

Replace the fixed colours, tints and gradients in the shell's own rules with names, add the block quote, rule and link rules for the assistant's markdown, and move the history chip to the wrapper with the masked icon.
Replace the fixed colours, tints, gradients and literal fallbacks in the row renderer's style with names, and give the decided badge its own passed and failed colours.
Point the chat's markdown tokens at names, replacing the fixed code ground.
Add the tests that keep fixed colours out and names defined, and update the four assertions that pinned the history chip's old fill and icon stroke.

migration.backwardCompat: No public interface changes. The exported names RENDER_REGISTRY_STYLE, CHAT_MARKDOWN_TOKENS and renderMarkdownStyle keep their types; no message, stored row or setting changes. A user sees the chat in their theme's colours from the next window reload after the update; there is no setting to keep the old dark palette.

alternativesConsidered.name: One named layer in the shell, pointed at theme variables
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: Keep the shell's named variables as the single place colours are chosen, point each at a --vscode-* variable, and replace every remaining literal with one of those names.
alternativesConsidered.approach: The shell's `:root` rule stays the one place where the chat's colours are chosen, but each name now holds a theme variable (for example the panel ground holds the editor background) and new names are added for the surfaces the mapping needs (widget surface, code-block ground, user-message ground and border, warning ground and border, button and secondary button, passed and failed, the four terminal colours, focus, dropdown, checkbox, progress, block quote, separator). The rules in the shell, in the row renderer's style and in the chat's markdown tokens keep referring to names; every hex, rgba and gradient outside `:root` is replaced by a name, and the forced dark colour scheme is removed. A test reads the rendered shell and fails on any fixed colour.

alternativesConsidered.name: Theme variables written directly in every rule
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: Remove the shell's named variables and write the --vscode-* variable in each rule that needs a colour.
alternativesConsidered.approach: The `:root` palette is deleted. Every rule in the shell's style, the row renderer's style and the chat's markdown tokens is rewritten to name the theme variable it uses directly, with the two-step fallbacks (user message, high-contrast border) repeated wherever they apply. The same test guards against fixed colours.
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: Meets the constraints but rewrites about 130 uses and repeats the fallback chains, so two elements of the same role can drift apart.

alternativesConsidered.name: Extend the shared token sheet and use it for the chat
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: Grow design-tokens.ts to cover every role the chat needs and make the chat use those --it-* tokens.
alternativesConsidered.approach: The shared terminal token set, which already maps nine roles to theme variables with literal fallbacks, is extended with the roles the chat needs, and the chat shell, row renderer and chat markdown tokens are changed to use the --it-* names instead of the shell's own. The docs-review panel, which uses the same sheet, receives the new tokens too.
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: Breaks two of the approved constraints: it changes a sheet the docs-review panel uses, and that sheet's pattern is a fixed literal fallback.

openQuestions: Which font should the assistant's markdown prose use? Today it is the one place in the chat that is not monospace: it uses a fixed sans stack ('Inter', system-ui, ...), while the approved spec says fonts are the theme's monospace editor font. Options: the VS Code interface font (--vscode-font-family), which keeps prose proportional as it is today and follows the user's settings (the design's default); or the editor's monospace font for prose too, as the spec's wording says.
